newsitem.title: INDIA: Doctors fix Mother Teresa's heartbeat.
newsitem.headline: Doctors fix Mother Teresa's heartbeat.

text.p: Doctors said they gave Mother Teresa a mild electric shock on Wednesday to correct her irregular heartbeat.

Dr Patricia Aubanel, part of the eight-member team treating the 86-year-old Roman Catholic nun, said the procedure was a success and the ailing missionary asked afterwards if she could return home from hospital.
Doctors had postponed the procedure, called cardioversion, at the weekend so Mother Teresa could regain more strength from heart surgery last month.

"It was mild electric shock and it lasted for a few seconds," Dr Tarun Praharaj said. "She was under sedation and the entire procedure was over within an hour, and we have to observe her for a minimum of 48 hours now."
Doctors said the procedure, during which a shock pad attached to a machine was placed on Mother Teresa's chest, was carried out at 10:30 a.m. (0500 GMT).
"At this point, she is stable and it is hoped that the sinus (regular) rhythm will remain," Aubanel told reporters at Calcutta's B.M. Birla Heart Research Centre.
Mother Teresa, who was fitted with a heart pacemaker in 1989 and has had three heart operations in five years, last underwent cardioversion in August.
"Is it over? Did it work?" Aubanel quoted Mother Teresa as asking immediately after the cardioversion.
When she was told it was a success, Mother Teresa said: "Wonderful. Let us go home now."
The 1979 Nobel Peace Prize winner had surgery on November 29 to clear two blocked coronary arteries. She had similar surgery in 1991 in the United States and in 1993 at the Birla clinic.

Her recovery this time has been complicated by bronchial pneumonia. Doctors said on Tuesday that Mother Teresa had had bronchitis for a long time and had built up resistance to many antibiotics used to combat the illness.
But they said they had finally found the right antibiotic.
"Mother Teresa's condition slightly improved today," her doctors said in a medical update on Wednesday before the cardioversion, noting that she had slept well and her condition was stabilising.

Mother Teresa had been reluctant to undergo "mechanical" cardioversion involving an electric shock, and doctors had said they would first use drugs. It was not known whether they had first tried drugs on Wednesday before administering the shock.

The revered Roman Catholic missionary has been pressing doctors to let her return to her Missionaries of Charity religious order to resume her work with the sick and dying, which has won her the title "Saint of the Gutters".
But doctors have cautioned that her recovery will be slow, and she might never be as active as before.
